title: Latency oddities — daily scrub & on-call follow-through (2027-11-03)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures the on-call summary for 2027-11-03 focused on intermittent tail latency spikes observed on the hosted API cluster (us-west-2, model: rdx-13b-quant). Notes include the timeline, mitigation steps taken during the shift, follow-ups for the next shift, and suggested runbook edits. Intention: handoff a concise, actionable set of context items for the daytime SRE rotation.

What happened (short):
- Between 02:20–03:10 UTC we saw several 95th/99th percentile token-latency spikes affecting the rdx-13b-quant endpoint.
- Root symptoms: CPU-steep backpressure on workers handling long-context requests (>4k tokens) and increased kernel preemption cycles reported on the inference hosts.
- Errors: no client 5xx surge; error-rate stable. But request queuing increased and client-visible tail latency spiked to ~1.2s per token in bursts (baseline ~0.35s).

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:15: Pager triggered for 99th percentile token latency (SLO boundary).
- 02:17: On-call (Maya) acked; triage started. Quick look at Grafana panel (linked) showed bursty correlation with long-context traffic.
- 02:25: Rolled a temporary route-weight shift: route 13b-quant -> fallback to 13b-int8 for non-latency-critical tenants. Noted ~10% traffic shift.
- 02:35: Deployed a hotfix config to reduce max-concurrency per worker from 32 -> 20 for affected pool. This reduced per-host queuing but increased overall worker count; autoscaler behavior observed.
- 02:48: Tail latency subsided to ~0.45s per token.
- 03:05: Observed a second smaller spike coinciding with a KV-cache miss storm (prefix caching TTL expirations aligned).
- 03:12: Cache TTL stagger applied (temporary): +random-jitter to prefix TTL expiry via feature-flag.
- 03:20: System stabilized; full handover prep started.

Immediate mitigations (what we did):
- Route-level fallbacks to lower-quantized model for non-critical tenants (manual override).
- Reduced per-worker concurrency for the affected GPU pool (config change).
- Staggered KV-cache TTLs to avoid synchronized expiries (feature-flag rollout).
- Monitoring: created a short-lived alert rule to track KV cache miss-rate and worker-queue-length together (to catch recurrence).

Observations / hypotheses:
- Hypothesis A: Long-context requests produce disproportionate KV cache churn (large KV cache invalidations and rehydration) that, combined with high concurrency, leads to backpressure in the runtime scheduler.
- Hypothesis B: Autoscaler latency and gradual worker spin-up caused transient under-provisioning during spike onset — queue length grew faster than new pods/hosts could join, amplifying token latency.
- Hypothesis C: Kernel scheduling preemption on a small subset of hosts (see host host-uw2-13 log snippet) correlated with higher CPU steal and elevated tail latency. Might be host-level noise (maintenance, container runtime GC).

Data & artifacts to review (for next shift):
- Correlate request-context-length distribution with per-request KV-cache hit/miss and token-latency (Grafana dashboard).
- Host-level /proc/stat & dmesg around spike windows for hosts with high preemption counts.
- Autoscaler event logs: check time-to-scale and any failed scale attempts between 02:10–02:40.
- Dump a sample of requests (anonymized) that hit 99th percentile (use sampling tool: gha/sre-sampler v0.7).

Runbook updates suggested (quick draft lines):
- Add a new section: "Long-context KV-cache churn" with steps: identify sustained cache miss-rate > X, apply TTL jitter, reduce worker concurrency by Y%, consider temporary route fallback.
- Document safe rollback steps for TTL-jitter feature-flag and how to revert route-weight changes.
- Add a check: before changing per-worker concurrency, verify autoscaler target can sustain the extra workers (instructions + CLI snippet).

Open action items (owners & ETA):
- (Alden) Investigate host kernel preemption logs, produce host list and potential remediation (ETA: 2027-11-04 end of day).
- (Priya) Run autoscaler slow-path analysis and produce timeline of scale events; propose fast-path tuning (ETA: 2027-11-05).
- (Maya) Draft runbook section for "KV-cache churn + long-context" and PR to Confluence (ETA: 2027-11-04 morning).
- (Eng-sre) Create a synthetic load test for long-context + heavy concurrent tokenize to reproduce locally (ETA: next sprint, owner TBD).

Notes for next on-call (handoff bullets):
- Watch the new temporary alert "kv-miss + queue-length correlation" (thresholds: kv-miss-rate > 0.12 AND queue-length > 300). If it fires: first apply TTL jitter flag (step documented below), then reduce worker concurrency.
- If latency reappears despite mitigations, escalate to infra-hosting (ticket JIRA-INC-3421) to check for kernel-level interference.
- Avoid broad rollback of route-weight changes; prefer staged reversion and monitor per-tenant error/latency.

Quick run commands (reference):
- Check queue length: curl -s http://ops-api.internal/pool/13b-quant/queue | jq .length
- Toggle TTL jitter flag: ./ffctl set kv_ttl_jitter=true --env=prod --pool=13b
- Reduce concurrency: infractl set-concurrency --pool=13b-quant --concurrency=20 --note "oncall emergency 2027-11-03"

Unresolved questions / follow-ups for postmortem:
- Why did TTL expiries align across hosts? Are we missing entropy in TTL calculation or was there an operator action earlier?
- Does the runtime scheduler expose metrics granular enough to distinguish KV rehydration CPU cost vs attention kernel cost?
- Are there specific tenants/prefixes that create disproportionate cache churn?

Misc notes (informal):
- Thank you to Alden for the quick host log correlation — saved a lot of noisy digging.
- The fallback-to-int8 route worked well for non-critical tenants; we should consider making that a documented policy for busy windows.

Handover status:
- System: STABLE (as of 03:30 UTC)
- Open pages/alerts: one newly-created alert (kv-miss + queue-length correlation) in state: active->resolved (auto-resolved after TTL jitter).
- Action queue: owners listed above; please update the doc when you start a task.

References / links (again):
- Grafana latency dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/abcd1234/latency-overview?orgId=1
- Autoscaler events: https://k8s-logs.redwood.internal/query?job=autoscaler&from=2027-11-03T02:00:00Z&to=2027-11-03T04:00:00Z
- JIRA: JIRA-INC-3421 (latency spike, hosts under review)

— Maya (on-call, 02:10–04:00 UTC)
